slides.title: Beyond a good story
slides.subtitle:
What 1.45 million Kiva loan descriptions
can and cannot tell us about funding speed
slides.visual: White ground; three photos (Kiva farmer, Unsplash market seller and tailor) in rounded frames; one yellow block and one violet offset

notes.purpose: Introduce the question and who we are.
notes.script: We are Cultural Blend, one of eight finalist teams in the UNSW Marketing Analytics Hackathon. We analysed 1.45 million Kiva loans to ask whether the way a borrower's story is written is linked to how fast the loan funds.
notes.reference: Portfolio edition, November 2026. Official results: unsw.edu.au MA-hackathon page (reviewed 2026-10-24). slides.title: Text carries forecast information, but no writing tip is proven
slides.subtitle: Summary across the explanatory models, robustness checks and forecast benchmark

body.heading: Uncertainty first
body.text: Yellow squares: significant terms that lost significance once errors were clustered by 48 countries.

body.heading: Most framing links are small
body.text: Five framings stay inside the ±5% band per extra mention per 100 words; urgency does not.

body.heading: Text adds forecast information
body.text: Text lowered linear forecast error every year, by 0.26–0.39 days; the median is about 7 hours.

notes.purpose: Give the answer before the detail.
notes.script: Three findings. First, the size of the data hid how uncertain many results were: once we accounted for countries, more than half the significant terms fell away. Second, most framing associations are small enough to bound, but urgency is too noisy to judge either way. Third, text does improve forecasts, by about a quarter to two fifths of a day. So text is informative, but we cannot yet say that changing it helps. [Point: Next decision] The next step is measurement and one small pilot.
notes.reference: claims_register.md rows: 64 of 120 (explanatory models, 2026-08-31 run); equivalence test (2026-11-08); forecast benchmark linear gains (2026-11-02).

slides.decision: Next decision: validate the text measures, then test one truthful prompt with partners.

slides.title: The description is one of the few listing fields still editable
slides.subtitle: Illustrative listing: what is fixed and what is editable when a loan is listed

exhibit.description: She has a banana stall at the market to support her family. She wants to buy more stock quickly, before prices rise. She is thankful to every lender who helps her business grow.
exhibit.caption: Illustrative composite listing, not a real borrower; values are dataset medians and most common categories.

takeaways.heading: The description is the editable part
takeaways.text: Most fields are fixed. The **description can still be edited**, so if framing mattered, wording guidance would be a cheap lever.

takeaways.heading: Eight framing rates, every loan
takeaways.text: **Eight framing rates per 100 words**, plus sentiment and text form, across 1,453,840 loans.

takeaways.heading: The test is for whom and when
takeaways.text: Which framings are linked to **faster funding**, for which loans, and when?

takeaways.heading: Pronouns reflect who writes
takeaways.text: Descriptions are mostly **written about the borrower, not by them**, so pronouns may reflect partner conventions.

notes.purpose: Show what a writer can and cannot change.
notes.script: This card is an illustrative composite, not a real borrower. Most of a listing is fixed by the time it goes live: amount, term, sector, country and partner. The description is the part someone can still edit. [Point: Eight framing rates, every loan] We counted framing words like these per 100 words, for family, business, urgency, gratitude and more, across every loan. [Point: Pronouns reflect who writes] These texts are usually written about the borrower by partner staff, so pronouns tell us more about who writes than about the borrower. [Point: The test is for whom and when] The question is which of these framings are linked to faster funding, for whom and when.

slides.title: The outcome is platform funding time, not borrower waiting time
slides.subtitle: Descriptive audit of all records

body.text: 1,453,846 input records; 6 negative durations excluded; 1,637 refunded records included.

takeaways.heading: Partners wait, not borrowers
takeaways.text: **96.4% of loans** reached the borrower a median 24.2 days before listing; platform time plausibly reflects replenishing partner capital.

takeaways.heading: Unfunded loans are missing
takeaways.text: Only loans that **eventually funded** are in the data, so we cannot study whether a loan funds at all.

takeaways.heading: We measure platform speed
takeaways.text: Our outcome runs from **listing to full funding**, median 2.85 days; it is not funding success or borrower welfare.

notes.purpose: Set the limits every later claim inherits.
notes.script: Our outcome is the time from listing to full funding, which takes a median of under three days. [Point: Partners wait, not borrowers] For almost all loans the partner paid the borrower about three weeks before the listing went live, so a faster platform fill plausibly helps the partner replenish capital rather than a waiting borrower. We do not observe that last step directly. [Point: Unfunded loans are missing] And the data only contain loans that funded.
notes.reference: 96.4% and 24.2 days: docs/1_data_dictionary.md (disbursalDate audit). Median 2.85 days, IQR 0.39–15.95: feature cache, 1,453,840 eligible records (2026-11-08). Counts: association_summary.txt and features.metadata.json.

slides.title: Same-day funding fell from 46.0% to 30.3% and stayed low through 2024
slides.subtitle: Share of loans fully funded within 24 hours, by posting year; descriptive

exhibit.caption: Share of completed loans funded within 24 hours, by posting year, with period averages.
exhibit.note: 2025 may be incomplete: loans still unfunded at extraction are missing.

takeaways.heading: The drop came in one year
takeaways.text: Same-day funding fell from **42.5% in 2019 to 32.3% in 2020**.

takeaways.heading: The low level held four years
takeaways.text: From 2021 to 2024 the share stayed **between 27.5% and 29.9%**; the 2025 rise may reflect an incomplete year.

takeaways.heading: Every model controls for period
takeaways.text: The shift is platform-wide, so **narrative effects are compared within periods**, not across them.

takeaways.heading: Causes are untested here
takeaways.text: Possible drivers, such as lender supply or listing volume, are **not measured** in this analysis.

notes.purpose: Show the market context.
notes.script: Before 2020 roughly 43 to 49 percent of loans funded within a day. [Point: The drop came in one year] The share fell sharply in 2020 and stayed under 30 percent through 2024. 2025 looks higher, but loans that had not funded by the time the data were extracted are missing, so that year may look faster than it was. [Point: Every model controls for period] Because the change is platform-wide, every model compares narratives within periods. [Point: Causes are untested here] We do not know why it happened; lender supply and listing volume are not in our data.

slides.subtitle: One dataset; the equivalence test builds on the robustness checks, and the forecast benchmark asks a separate question

exhibit.source: Kiva loans, 2016–2025: 1,453,840 valid completed durations in 48 countries

steps.question: Do the links survive richer controls?
steps.method: The same models with more text measures and a programme proxy; multiple-test adjusted.
steps.headline: Only small associations remain

notes.purpose: Explain how the evidence fits together.
notes.script: All four analyses use the same loans. The explanatory models ask which features are linked to speed, and how sure we can be. The robustness checks rerun them with richer controls, and the equivalence test then asks which of those links are small enough to bound. [Point: Forecast benchmark] The forecast benchmark asks a different question: does text help predict funding time? Its numbers are not comparable with the others. [Point: Years each analysis uses] The strip at the bottom shows the years: the explanatory work uses all loans, the holdout tests on 2024 and 2025, and the benchmark retrains five times, each time only on loans completed before the test year. [Point: What each can claim] Each analysis supports a different kind of claim, and none of them is causal.

slides.title: Large row counts did not remove country-level uncertainty
slides.subtitle: Explanatory models: HC3 versus 48-country clustered errors

takeaways.heading: Text terms are hit hardest
takeaways.text: **42 of 56 text terms** lost significance, against 22 of 64 control terms.

takeaways.heading: Urgency no longer passes
takeaways.text: Its p-value rose from below 0.001 to **0.49** for funding time and 0.22 for same-day funding.

takeaways.heading: Few countries dominate
takeaways.text: Ten countries hold **81% of loans**, so the 48 weigh like about 5.7 equal-sized ones.

takeaways.heading: Weak evidence is not no effect
takeaways.text: **Losing significance is not evidence of no effect**; the next slide tests that directly.

notes.purpose: Show why we distrust headline significance.
notes.script: With 1.45 million rows almost everything looks significant. When we let errors correlate within each of 48 countries, 64 of the 120 significant terms fell away. [Point: Text terms are hit hardest] Most of those are text terms: 42 of 56, against 22 of 64 controls. [Point: Urgency no longer passes] Urgency is the clearest case. [Point: Few countries dominate] The reason is concentration: ten countries hold 81 percent of loans. [Point: Weak evidence is not no effect] That tells us the evidence is weak, not that the effect is zero.
notes.reference: Explanatory models, primary saved run 2026-08-31: association_summary.txt; split by src/clustering_split.py (reports/evidence_sources/clustering_split.json); shares by src/country_shares.py.

slides.title: Most framing associations are small; urgency remains unresolved
slides.subtitle: Equivalence test of the robustness-check coefficients; exploratory, bound set after the estimates

exhibit.unit: change in log(1 + days) per extra mention per 100 words, 90% interval, expanded specification

takeaways.heading: Five framings are small
takeaways.text: Five framings stay **inside ±5% of funding time** in both specifications.

takeaways.heading: Urgency and first person are unknown
takeaways.text: Urgency and first-person framing could still be linked to **6–14% faster or slower funding** per mention. Each is absent from over 98% of records.

takeaways.heading: The bound came after the data
takeaways.text: The bound was chosen **after seeing the estimates**; a confirmatory test needs one agreed in advance.

takeaways.heading: The verdicts survive a stricter test
takeaways.text: With a stricter t(4) reference, **all five duration verdicts still hold**.

notes.purpose: Separate 'small' from 'unknown'.
notes.script: The shaded band is a practical bound, about five percent of funding time per extra mention. When a whole interval sits inside the band, we can say the association is small. Most framings do. Urgency and first person do not: their intervals are wide enough to allow sizeable links either way. [Point: The bound came after the data] We chose the bound after seeing the results, so treat this as exploratory. Edit size matters too: one mention in a typical description is a realistic edit, but almost no descriptions contain these words, so the data say little about them.
notes.reference: Equivalence test run 2026-11-08. reports/equivalence_screen_reviewed/README.md; src/equivalence.py. Edit-size context: reports/equivalence_screen_reviewed/feature_distribution.json.

slides.title: Regional family-framing patterns rest on two countries each
slides.subtitle: Explanatory models: within-region slopes with country-clustered and heuristic few-cluster intervals

exhibit.unit: change in log(1 + days) per extra family mention per 100 words

takeaways.heading: Two countries cannot make a pattern
takeaways.text: With two clusters, between-country uncertainty **cannot be estimated well**; the heuristic intervals cross zero.

takeaways.heading: No regional writing rules
takeaways.text: These are descriptive patterns, **not grounds for country or regional writing rules**.

takeaways.heading: More countries would settle it
takeaways.text: A regional test needs **more countries per region**, or partner-level data.

notes.purpose: Prevent over-reading the most striking regional result.
notes.script: Family framing looks linked to faster funding in two regions. But each region is two countries. A t(1) screen, which is a heuristic and not a calibrated test, widens the intervals across zero.
notes.reference: Explanatory models, primary saved run 2026-08-31. docs/2_evidence_and_corrections.md regional table.

slides.title: Few narrative associations remain after programme controls
slides.subtitle: Robustness checks: country-clustered, BH-adjusted within specification

exhibit.note: Per extra mention per 100 words; BH-adjusted within each specification.

takeaways.heading: Only small associations remain
takeaways.text: Third-person framing keeps its size but rises to **BH p 0.061**; business framing is **the one term below BH 0.05**.

takeaways.heading: These are still associations
takeaways.text: Programme text is an **unvalidated proxy**; neither result shows what editing would do.

takeaways.heading: Pronouns may reflect the writer
takeaways.text: Descriptions are usually written by partners, so the **third-person link may reflect who writes**, not a borrower's choice.

notes.purpose: Show that not everything disappears.
notes.script: Few results remain under richer controls. Third-person framing keeps about the same size, but its adjusted p-value rises just above 0.05. Business framing is the one term that passes after programme controls, with a slightly lower same-day rate. Both are small and observational. [Point: Pronouns may reflect the writer] Descriptions are usually written by partner staff, so the third-person link may say more about who writes than about the borrower.

key_figures.label: third-person BH p, expanded to programme-adjusted

slides.title: Adding text lowered forecast error in 5 of 5 years
slides.subtitle: Forecast benchmark: linear model, structure only versus structure plus text, identical evaluation rows

takeaways.heading: Text carries forecast information
takeaways.text: Gains of **0.26–0.39 days** on 728,640 evaluation records.

takeaways.heading: Forecasting is not persuasion
takeaways.text: Text may encode **purpose, place or programme templates**, not only persuasion.

takeaways.heading: No single country drives it
takeaways.text: Removing any single country **leaves the gain positive** in every year (exploratory check).

notes.purpose: Present the strongest new result.
notes.script: We trained on earlier years and tested on each of 2021 to 2025, comparing the same model with and without text on the same loans. Text reduced error every year.

slides.title: The gain is modest and depends on the model
slides.subtitle: Forecast benchmark: annual MAE gain with month-resampled 95% intervals

series.name: Linear, adds form, lexicon and TF-IDF

takeaways.heading: The tree model gains little
takeaways.text: The tree model, without TF-IDF, gains **at most 0.04 days**.

takeaways.heading: Country intervals are wide
takeaways.text: Country resampling **includes zero in 4 of 5** linear years. Capping extreme forecasts, an exploratory check, leaves zero in 1 of 5.

takeaways.heading: Metrics move in different directions
takeaways.text: In 2025 text improved error and calibration but **AUC fell** from 0.893 to 0.888.

notes.purpose: Keep the gain in proportion.
notes.script: The linear gains are consistent month to month, but country resampling is less kind, and the tree model gains little. [Point: Country intervals are wide] Part of that country fragility comes from a few extreme forecasts: when we cap forecasts at the longest training wait, an exploratory check, the country interval excludes zero in 4 of 5 years. Different metrics also move in different directions.
notes.reference: docs/6_matched_text_results.md; reports/loss_alignment_2025/README.md (all five years, capped diagnostic).

slides.title: Three gates before any writing advice
slides.subtitle: Proposed next research for Kiva and participating partners; each gate must pass before the next

steps.name: Validate the measures
steps.question: Do our word counts capture clarity, need and agency?
steps.do: Build a small codebook; two people code the same narratives and resolve disagreements.
steps.done: Definitions are frozen before later periods are checked.

steps.name: Close the data gaps
steps.question: What did lenders see, and which listings never funded?
steps.do: Get original texts, partner identifiers, exposure data and expired listings.
steps.done: Unfunded listings and listing-time text are in the data.

steps.name: Pilot one prompt
steps.question: Does editing a description change funding speed?
steps.do: With partners, test one truthful clarity prompt against a control.
steps.done: Threshold, power and guardrails are agreed in advance.

notes.purpose: End on a decision path.
notes.script: Before anyone tells borrowers how to write, three things need to happen, in order. First, check that our word counts measure what we think. Second, get the data we are missing: what lenders saw and the listings that never funded. Third, test one truthful prompt with partners. [Point: Each gate unlocks a stronger claim] Each gate lets us say a little more, from associations today to a tested effect of editing. If a gate fails, we stop and report the uncertainty.
notes.reference: docs/6_matched_text_results.md, What to do next; docs/4_research_review.md.

body.heading: Why two countries are not enough
body.text: A one-country group cannot estimate between-country uncertainty, and two countries estimate it poorly. The t(1) reference keeps the same clustered standard error and widens the interval.

body.heading: What the screen is
body.text: A heuristic sensitivity screen, not a calibrated correction. Passing it would not certify a result, so these patterns stay descriptive.

notes.purpose: Show the regional screen in full.
notes.script: This is the detail behind the regional slide. With two countries per region, the usual interval is too narrow, and the t(1) screen shows how much it could widen.
